The folder `data/` holds the data behind a published data story, "The Unlikely Odds of Making it Big": https://pudding.cool/2017/01/making-it-big/
The files: data/web_data.csv, data/web_venues.csv, data/web_made.csv

Write down the story's findings that this data reproduces.

1. Read the story on the web. web_fetch returns the page as the server sends it. web_view opens it in a browser and scrolls it like a reader, so it also gets text drawn by scripts, chart labels and the text of scrolling steps: use it when web_fetch returns little of the story, and to read what the charts label. Follow links to the story's methods or data notes when they say how a number was computed.
2. List every finding the authors draw from data: each number, comparison, ranking, share, trend or pattern the text states or a chart labels. A description of the data itself is not a finding: how many records, people, items, categories or sources it has, and how it was collected. When a chart states the same thing for each of its items (the top three for each phrase, the share for each year), that is one finding, written as one fact whose code computes it for every item at once.
3. Write each finding the files in data/ can reproduce as a fact in `facts.json`:

```json
[{"id": "women-front-shorter",
  "source": "On average, the pockets in women's jeans are 48% shorter and 6.5% narrower than men's pockets.",
  "claim": "Women's front pockets average 14.3 cm of maximum height against 23.1 cm for men.",
  "tables": {"m": "data/measurements.csv"},
  "code": "m.groupby('menWomen').maxHeightFront.mean()"}]
```

- `id`: unique in the file, a few meaningful words.
- `source`: the story's own words for this finding, quoted exactly, from its text or a chart label.
- `claim`: the finding in one sentence, with the numbers the code prints, and nothing the printout does not show: the story's own wording and numbers belong in `source`, not in the claim.
- `tables`: the files the code reads, each a variable name and the file's path from this folder, such as `data/orders.csv`; every file is read with `pd.read_csv(path)`.
- `code`: one Python expression over those variables, with `pd` (pandas) and `np` (numpy) available: the plain pandas computation whose printout shows the finding, such as a filter, a group-by, a count, a share or a sort. Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict.

Evaluate every fact from this folder the way it will be checked: read its `tables` with `pd.read_csv`, evaluate its `code`, print the value the way pandas prints it, and read the printout against the claim and the source. Every number, name and comparison in the claim must be in the printout, computed from the tables: code that writes a number itself, such as a string or a Series of typed-in values, does not count. The printout must agree with the story's numbers, up to rounding. Use the story's own definitions and filters, from its text or methods: a term means the same in every fact (if making it past the rookie contract is more than two seasons in one fact, it is more than two seasons in all of them), and a range, threshold or subset is one the story uses, never one chosen to make a number come out right. If the story's number only comes out under a definition or filter the story does not use, the finding is not reproduced. If after a fair try the data does not give the story's number (it needs other data, a different period, or the numbers differ beyond rounding), leave the finding out of facts.json.

4. Write `skipped.json`: every finding you left out, as [{"source": "the story's words", "why": "..."}].

Deliver both files, even when the data reproduces none of the story's findings: then `facts.json` is `[]`.
I'll start by exploring the data folder and reading the story.

The Unlikely Odds of Making it Big
3,180 bands that played multiple shows from 2013-2016
The Pudding
The unlikely odds of
#
Making it big
What three years and 75,000 shows in New York tell us about the chance
your favorite band will succeed.
By
Russell Samora &
Dan Kopf
On July 17, 2013, the band Sylvan Esso headlined the 250 person capacity Mercury Lounge. Sylvan Esso was one of over 7,000 bands to play a small show in the NYC area
that year. The duo had just released their debut singles Play it Right and Hey Mami. The band had some buzz,
but hyped indie bands often come and go.
Sylvan Esso was not one of them. About two years later, they headlined a sold-out show at Terminal 5 — a
3,000 person capacity venue in NYC. There could be little doubt that Sylvan Esso had “made it”.
In the video below, you can see thousands of Sylvan Esso fans sing along to the playful synth-pop of “Hey
Mami”.
“That was crazy.” Sylvan Esso’s beat-maker Nick Sanborn told the Village Voice after the show. “I don’t know how to put stuff like that into
perspective… I think we both just feel really lucky that people get what we’re trying to say.”
Sanborn was right to feel amazed. What happened to his band is rare.
According to data from the music event website Songkick, of the 7,000 bands that headlined a small venue (less than 700 capacity)
in the NYC area in 2013, less than half even played another show from 2014 to October of 2016.
Of the bands that did play again, only 400 of them headlined a show at
a venue with a capacity greater than 700 people.
But only 21 out of the 7,000 bands reached Sylvan Esso’s level of “making
it”: headlining a show of over 3,000 capacity. Any act that headlines a venue of this size has reached a
level of success that they could have barely dreamed of (with the possible exception of Kanye West). The
following list shows some of the 21 bands who made it, and when and where they hit it big.
- A Great Big World
- Date: July 23, 2014
- Venue: Manhattan Center
- Sam Smith
- Date: September 18, 2014
- Venue: United Palace Theatre
- Bastille
- Date: October 9, 2014
- Venue: Radio City Music Hall
- Lake Street Dive
- Date: November 14, 2014
- Venue: Terminal 5
- Sylvan Esso
- Date: January 23, 2015
- Venue: Terminal 5
- London Grammar
- Date: January 27, 2015
- Venue: Terminal 5
- Chet Faker
- Date: April 04, 2015
- Venue: Terminal 5
- Chance the Rapper
- Date: October 23, 2015
- Venue: Terminal 5
- X Ambassadors
- Date: May 13, 2016
- Venue: Terminal 5
- Mayer Hawthorne
- Date: June 24, 2016
- Venue: Terminal 5
And the remaining 11 others who made it...
- 5 Seconds of Summer
- Chase Rice
- Disclosure
- Gorgon City
- Houndmouth
- Lucius
- Mac DeMarco
- Misterwives
- Rudimental
- Shakey Graves
- Sturgill Simpson
# How long it takes to make it
In terms of how quickly they “made it”, Sylvan Esso are an anomaly. The band rose faster than any other US
based band in our dataset—with less than two years between their first NYC show and headlining a big venue.
The long journey to popular success of the indie pop band Lucius is more typical. The Brooklyn based band
played 24 small to medium sized shows in New York from 2009 to 2014, before headlining Terminal Five in
December 2014.
The bands that make it from outside the U.S. are more likely to have short journeys to “making it”. Bands
like Bastille and Disclosure had already seen significant success in their homelands before making their
first appearance in the United States, and by the the time they returned for another tour they had really
hit it big.
Let’s look at the different paths each band took to make it, including shows they opened and shows they headlined .
# Everybody else
The vast majority of bands never do make it. Acts break up, give up or decide they have other things they
want to do with their lives.
For every Chance the Rapper there are thousands of rappers that never play a show with more than a couple
hundred people. For every Lake Street Dive, there are hundreds of promising bands that break up because they
lost on their members.
To see the NYC concert trajectory of different bands, below you can search for any
of the 3,000 bands that played a show in 2013 , and at least one more show from 2014 to 2016.
Perhaps some of them are on their way to making it, and it just hasn’t happened yet.

since most revenue comes from shows. The tiers of success (small, medium, and big) are manual thresholds that
seemed appropriate after analyzing the data. Get in touch: russell@pudding.cool or @russellviz.

Let me get the rest of the web_view content (the "how long it takes" chart labels etc.) and examine the data files thoroughly.

Key findings from the story:
1. "3,180 bands that played multiple shows from 2013-2016" — hmm, that's a data description (number of records)? Actually the title card states it. That's a description of the data, not a finding. But "of the 7,000 bands that headlined a small venue (less than 700 capacity) in the NYC area in 2013, less than half even played another show from 2014 to October of 2016." — that's a finding: bands headlining small venue in 2013 < 700 capacity; share that played again after. Need to compute.

2. "Of the bands that did play again, only 400 of them headlined a show at a venue with a capacity greater than 700 people." — finding.

3. "But only 21 out of the 7,000 bands reached Sylvan Esso's level of 'making it': headlining a show of over 3,000 capacity." — finding (21 out of ~7000; but wait, "7,000" is count of bands that headlined small venue in 2013; the 21 should be of the 7,000? In data web_made.csv has 24 rows? Let me check).

4. "Sylvan Esso ... rose faster than any other US based band in our dataset—with less than two years between their first NYC show and headlining a big venue." — finding (Sylvan Esso fastest US band, <2 years).

5. "Lucius ... played 24 small to medium sized shows in New York from 2009 to 2014, before headlining Terminal Five in December 2014." — finding (24 shows). And chart gives "5.3 years from their first small show in NYC until they made it big; Aug 16, 2009 Barbès (60); Dec 06, 2014 Terminal 5 (3,000)". Hmm the data likely starts 2013? Actually data has 2009? Order shows dates in 2013, 2016... Let me check. Data web_data seems limited to shows with an entry.

6. "The bands that make it from outside the U.S. are more likely to have short journeys" — qualitative.

7. Chart of time-to-make-it for bands: labels 4.6, 3.6, 3.5, 3.3, 3.0, 2.9, 2.5, 2.4, 2.3, 2.2, 1.8, 1.5, 1.4, 1.3, 1.2, 1.0 years for the 21 bands (or 16 shown?). That's a chart stating for each band the time from first small show to making it. Could be one finding computed for all bands: time between first small show and first big headlining show.

8. "Women-front"? no.

9. "Sylvan Esso was one of over 7,000 bands to play a small show in the NYC area that year." — finding? It's a data description (count). Hmm "over 7,000 bands to play a small show in NYC area in 2013". Later "7,000 bands that headlined a small venue (less than 700 capacity)". I'd treat counts a data description? The instructions: "A description of the data itself is not a finding: how many records, people, items, categories or sources it has, and how it was collected." So the 7,000 count is a data description? Hmm, but "of the 7,000 bands ... less than half even played another show" is a share finding. The 7,000 alone is a count of records, so probably skip as data description. But the "21 out of 7,000" is a share finding — the ratio matters.

Also "For every Chance the Rapper there are thousands of rappers that never play a show..." — rhetorical, maybe not data claim; "thousands" not checkable. Skip.

"played 24 small to medium sized shows in New York from 2009 to 2014" — data likely doesn't include 2009-2012 shows? Let's check. web_data.csv has 3180 bands; the dates might span multiple years. Actually Sylvan Esso's id 7274689 above had dates 2013-2016 only. Hmm but maybe overall more.

Let's inspect data.

Also web_made.csv — 24 rows (21? maybe 24 incl. duplicates). Let's look.

The Unlikely Odds of Making it Big
3,180 bands that played multiple shows from 2013-2016
The Pudding
The unlikely odds of
#
Making it big
What three years and 75,000 shows in New York tell us about the chance
your favorite band will succeed.
By
Russell Samora &
Dan Kopf
On July 17, 2013, the band Sylvan Esso headlined the 250 person capacity Mercury Lounge. Sylvan Esso was one of over 7,000 bands to play a small show in the NYC area
that year. The duo had just released their debut singles Play it Right and Hey Mami. The band had some buzz,
but hyped indie bands often come and go.
Sylvan Esso was not one of them. About two years later, they headlined a sold-out show at Terminal 5 — a
3,000 person capacity venue in NYC. There could be little doubt that Sylvan Esso had “made it”.
In the video below, you can see thousands of Sylvan Esso fans sing along to the playful synth-pop of “Hey
Mami”.
“That was crazy.” Sylvan Esso’s beat-maker Nick Sanborn told the Village Voice after the show. “I don’t know how to put stuff like that into
perspective… I think we both just feel really lucky that people get what we’re trying to say.”
Sanborn was right to feel amazed. What happened to his band is rare.
According to data from the music event website Songkick, of the 7,000 bands that headlined a small venue (less than 700 capacity)
in the NYC area in 2013, less than half even played another show from 2014 to October of 2016.
Of the bands that did play again, only 400 of them headlined a show at
a venue with a capacity greater than 700 people.
But only 21 out of the 7,000 bands reached Sylvan Esso’s level of “making
it”: headlining a show of over 3,000 capacity. Any act that headlines a venue of this size has reached a
level of success that they could have barely dreamed of (with the possible exception of Kanye West). The
following list shows some of the 21 bands who made it, and when and where they hit it big.

# How long it takes to make it
In terms of how quickly they “made it”, Sylvan Esso are an anomaly. The band rose faster than any other US
based band in our dataset—with less than two years between their first NYC show and headlining a big venue.
The long journey to popular success of the indie pop band Lucius is more typical. The Brooklyn based band
played 24 small to medium sized shows in New York from 2009 to 2014, before headlining Terminal Five in
December 2014.
The bands that make it from outside the U.S. are more likely to have short journeys to “making it”. Bands
like Bastille and Disclosure had already seen significant success in their homelands before making their
first appearance in the United States, and by the the time they returned for another tour they had really
hit it big.

The unlikely odds of
# Making it big
What three years and 75,000 shows in New York tell us about the chance your favorite band will succeed.
By [Russell Samora](https://twitter.com/russellviz)&[Dan Kopf](https://twitter.com/dkopf)
On July 17, 2013, the band Sylvan Esso headlined the 250 person capacity Mercury Lounge. Sylvan Esso was one of over 7,000 bands to play a small show in the NYC area that year. The duo had just released their debut singles [Play it Right](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xnBjwrRmo2U) and [Hey Mami](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3mh2RctlGxc). The band had some buzz, but hyped indie bands often come and go.
Sylvan Esso was not one of them. About two years later, they headlined a sold-out show at Terminal 5 — a 3,000 person capacity venue in NYC. There could be little doubt that Sylvan Esso had “made it”.
In the video below, you can see thousands of Sylvan Esso fans sing along to the playful synth-pop of “Hey Mami”.
[Video 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qftu7ZQieuw)
“That was crazy.” Sylvan Esso’s beat-maker Nick Sanborn [told the Village Voice](http://www.villagevoice.com/music/the-blissful-complicated-world-of-sylvan-esso-swings-back-through-brooklyn-7399764) after the show. “I don’t know how to put stuff like that into perspective… I think we both just feel really lucky that people get what we’re trying to say.”
Sanborn was right to feel amazed. What happened to his band is rare.
According to data from the music event website [Songkick](http://songkick.com/), of the 7,000 bands that headlined a small venue (less than 700 capacity) in the NYC area in 2013, less than half even played another show from 2014 to October of 2016.
Of the bands that did play again, only 400 of them headlined a show at a venue with a capacity greater than 700 people.
But only 21 out of the 7,000 bands reached Sylvan Esso’s level of “making it”: headlining a show of over 3,000 capacity. Any act that headlines a venue of this size has reached a level of success that they could have barely dreamed of (with the possible exception of Kanye West). The following list shows some of the 21 bands who made it, and when and where they hit it big.

## How long it takes to make it
In terms of how quickly they “made it”, Sylvan Esso are an anomaly. The band rose faster than any other US based band in our dataset—with less than two years between their first NYC show and headlining a big venue.
The long journey to popular success of the indie pop band Lucius is more typical. The Brooklyn based band played 24 small to medium sized shows in New York from 2009 to 2014, before headlining Terminal Five in December 2014.
The bands that make it from outside the U.S. are more likely to have short journeys to “making it”. Bands like Bastille and Disclosure had already seen significant success in their homelands before making their first appearance in the United States, and by the the time they returned for another tour they had really hit it big.
Let’s look at the different paths each band took to make it, including shows they opened and shows they headlined.
## Everybody else
The vast majority of bands never do make it. Acts break up, give up or decide they have other things they want to do with their lives.
For every Chance the Rapper there are thousands of rappers that never play a show with more than a couple hundred people. For every Lake Street Dive, there are hundreds of promising bands that break up because they lost on their members.

content.thinking:
The web_view scroll text includes the whole band list (huge), so chart labels only in first output. We have them.

Let's now think about whether the story has a methods/data notes link. The methodology paragraph only says tiers manual thresholds. No detailed computation. So no additional definitions.

Potential fact about "made it" list names: The story explicitly names 10 bands with dates/venues and 11 more. We can create a fact whose code computes, for every band in `web_made` that appears in the show data, the first headlining show at a venue of capacity >= 3000, and compare. But printout will include Mayer's MSG earlier. If claim says "Twenty-one bands reached a >=3,000-capacity headlining show; the first such shows include ..." with dates for the nine matching? That's messy.

Maybe the intended fact for the list is: "The 21 bands that made it are A Great Big World, Sam Smith, ..., Sturgill Simpson", i.e., the membership, not the dates. Code can get exactly those 21 by using the story's made.csv list and the data: `d[d.name.isin(made.name) & (d.tier==2)].name.sort_values()`. But that's 21 names, exactly. Claim: "The 21 bands that headlined a 3,000-capacity venue are [names]." This is computed from made.csv + web_data. Is it circular? The names come from made.csv, but the claim is that these 21 are the made bands. The code filters data by names in made.csv; not independent. Alternatively code: `d[(d.tier==2)&(d.value==1)].name` returns same 21, using value flag. Hmm.

Let's check whether `tier==2 & value==1` exactly equals made ∩ data.
